## Overview

The Akuntsu, also known as Akunt'su or Akunsu, are an Indigenous people of Rondônia, Brazil. Their land forms part of the Rio Omerê Indigenous Territory, a small Indigenous territory also inhabited by a group of Kanoê. The Akuntsu are primarily hunter-gatherers and supplement their diet with some swidden agriculture. Their reserve provides a refuge for game whose habitats have been destroyed by deforestation in the surrounding area. The Akuntsu language belongs to the Tuparí branch of the Tupari language family and is spoken only by members of the group, without being fully understood by outsiders. Their recent history includes violent attacks by cattle ranchers, loggers and colonists, official contact by FUNAI in 1995, and a severe population decline. The sources describe their language and culture as unlikely to survive after the deaths of the remaining members.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The Akuntsu language source gives *ororope* as the word for “clothes,” formed from *ororo*, “cotton,” and *pe*, “coating.” This linguistic example documents vocabulary and word formation.

### Architecture

The historical accounts state that an Akuntsu village inhabited by around 30 people was bulldozed after a massacre. They also record that, in January 2000, the youngest girl died when a tree fell on her father’s house during a storm. These references establish the existence of houses and a village.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The language source includes vocabulary examples such as *waʔi* (“stone”), *ororo* (“cotton”), *ep* (“leaf”), *op* (“father”), and *wako* (“jacu”), but these are presented as grammatical examples rather than catalogue descriptions of objects or technologies.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The historical source states that several survivors of the attack by armed cattle ranchers possessed scars and bullets lodged in their bodies.

## Music & performance

The language source documents grammatical examples involving *Konibú*, the shaman and chieftain named in the historical account, including the sentence translated as “Konibú hunted them.” This is linguistic evidence, not an account of musical performance.

## Dance & theatre

They mention various shamanic rituals.

## Festivals & rituals

They state that the Akuntsu practice various shamanic rituals, without explaining their names, sequence, participants, objects, or occasions.

The historical material does describe several events involving contact and death. FUNAI officially contacted the Akuntsu in October 1995, when the group numbered seven: two men, three adult women and two young girls. In January 2000, the youngest girl died when a tree fell on her father’s house during a storm. In October 2009, the oldest member, Ururú, died. In 2016, the shaman and chieftain Konibu died in his sleep, leaving three women—Babawru, Pugapia and Aiga—according to that account. A later passage states that on December 8, 2025, after three decades without registered births, a boy was born through the union of Babawru Akuntsú and Purá, from the Kanoê people.

## Foodways

The Akuntsu are primarily hunter-gatherers and supplement their diet with some swidden agriculture. Game is described as particularly abundant in their reserve because the protected area serves as a refuge for animals whose habitats have been destroyed by surrounding deforestation.

The Akuntsu language source gives *ko* as the verb “to eat,” which becomes *ka* in a particular verbal construction. It also gives *apara koara kom* as an example translated “I will eat bananas as usual.” These examples establish linguistic references to eating and bananas.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Akuntsu language is spoken only by members of the group and is not fully understood by outsiders. Its continued survival is considered unlikely after the deaths of the remaining members, and several observers have described the Akuntsu as victims of genocide.

## Language & religion

Akuntsú is a Tupian language of the Tupari branch, spoken in the state of Rondônia in Brazil. It is classified as belonging to the Tupari subfamily and is related to Tuparí, Kepkiriwát, Makuráp, Mekéns, Waratégaya and Wayoró. The language is most closely related to Mekéns among the languages listed, sharing approximately 79% of its vocabulary. The name “Akuntsú” is stated to come from the Kwaza language word *akucũ*, “outsider Indians,” while another account says that *Akuntsu* is an exonym applied by the Kanoê, meaning roughly “other Indians.”

The language has five vowels and distinguishes future from non-future through the projective marker *kom*. Its documented grammatical structure includes transitive and intransitive verbs, reduplication, clitic pronouns, postpositions, particles, and subject–object–verb as the default word order. The sources state that the Akuntsu practice various shamanic rituals.
